stories.title: Disruption in Dublin and Doonbeg as Trump set to visit
stories.summary:
There will be disruption in Dublin and Doonbeg as US President Donald Trump visits Ireland this weekend. He is expected to touch down on Air Force One at Dublin Airport tomorrow morning. There will be rolling road closures in place around the airport from 7.30am until 9.30am and between 11.30am and 1.30pm. Dublin Airport will operate as normal but passengers are being advised to allow extra time for their journey as they may not be able to access the airport via their usual route, and may need to take an alternative, potentially longer, route. Passengers are advised to use traffic apps and check the latest updates from TII and GardaTraffic before travelling. Passenger Advice - Saturday 12th Sept

stories.summary: An unpublished Health Service Executive (HSE) internal review obtained by the programme also raised concerns about the culture and leadership of the service, including references to bullying and harassment and what it described as a traditional "command and control" management style. The report, carried out by the HSE's Workplace Health and Wellbeing Unit, has not previously been published or reported on. Documents obtained by Prime Time also show that concerns about misogyny, gender discrimination and sexual harassment were raised with the Director of the NAS Robert Morton by senior management. The women who spoke to the programme include current and former paramedics and emergency medical technicians. Many spoke anonymously because they continue to work in the service. They stressed that there are many good people working within NAS, including many men, but described what they believe is a long-standing culture in which inappropriate behaviour was tolerated and complaints were not always properly addressed. NAS is a part of the HSE in which more than 2,400 staff are employed nationwide.

stories.title: Tánaiste says savings in Budget will help families
stories.summary: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance Simon Harris has said that hundreds of euros saved in the Budget in relation to income tax will help families. Speaking after a Fine Gael think-in in Amber Springs Hotel Gorey, Co Wexford he was asked about the impact of inflation in light of the ECB rate hike. People want to know Government "gets it," he said, noting that the Budget was "25 days away, I think tomorrow". Mr Harris wants to see the Budget "as an opportunity to reset on a number of big issues that I think the Irish people want to see us make progress on". He wants to make "sure that people who work hard can get ahead of this country and not just get by making progress, not in a temporary way but in a structural way". He said the Budget must be seen in the round and as one of four budgets.

stories.title: UK economy grows at fastest pace since February 2025
stories.summary: The UK economy grew at the fastest annual pace in 18 months in July, helped by a boost from artificial intelligence and extending a strong first-half performance despite headwinds from the US-Iran war, official figures showed today. British gross domestic product in July was 1.6% higher than a year earlier, the fastest annual rate since February 2025 and above economists' 1.2% forecast, the Office for National Statistics figures showed today. The economy grew 0.4% on the month in July, compared with median expectations in a Reuters poll for output to be unchanged, and output in the three months to July - which smooths volatility - was also stronger than expected at 0.4%. Much of the growth over the past three months appeared to come from businesses involved in computer programming that were benefiting from the AI boom, the ONS' Director of Economic Statistics, Liz McKeown, said. "Looking at the latest month, services also drove growth in July, with computer programming again making the largest contribution," she added, noting an extra boost for some firms from the men's soccer World Cup and unusually hot weather. Sterling was little changed against the US dollar after the data and economists had mixed views about whether Britain's current economic outperformance would be sustained in the run-up to finance minister John Healey's first budget next month.

stories.title: Man who checked in 9/11 hijackers 'didn't listen' to gut
stories.summary: As an airline customer service agent, Michael Tuohey helped two of the hijackers check into their flights at Portland International Jetport in Maine on 11 September 2001 - the starting point of a journey that ended in American Airlines Flight 11 crashing into the North Tower of the World Trade Centre. Another jet flew into the South Tower, followed by a third that went into the Pentagon and a fourth downed in Pennsylvania killed about 3,000 people. The day amounted to an unprecedented attack that left behind tens of thousands of grieving spouses, parents and children and stunned the world. The events of September 11th, early in President George W Bush's first term, profoundly reshaped US national security policy and led to decades-long wars in which more than 900,000 died - primarily in Iraq and Afghanistan. They also changed the course of individual lives, inspiring some children of victims to follow their parents into emergency service, steering others toward military, medical or public-service careers, and leaving survivors, responders and millions of Americans still reckoning with the legacy of that day. A routine morning for Mr Tuohey in New England changed when Mohammad Atta and Abdul Aziz al Omari arrived just a half hour before their flight.

stories.title: Carrick knows tougher tests coming after Sabah cakewalk
stories.summary: Michael Carrick enjoyed Manchester United's perfect Champions League return against Sabah but is "pushing for more" with tougher tests around the corner. Thursday night saw Old Trafford host a first match in European football’s premier competition since December 2023 as the Red Devils faced a club that were only founded nine years ago. United ran out comfortable 4-0 victors against Sabah, the champions of Azerbaijan, with Matheus Cunha, Bruno Fernandes and Benjamin Sesko scoring first-half goals. Lisandro Martinez tapped home to complete a blemish-free start to the league phase for Carrick’s men, who recorded their first clean sheet of the season having made a topsy-turvy start to the Premier League. Asked if Thursday was the perfect way to kick off their long-awaited Champions League return, the United head coach said: "Yeah, I think so. "Kind of what we set out to achieve, really. I think it was a good performance, individually, collectively, pretty much all the way through the game, from start to finish.

stories.title: Something for the Weekend: Piers McGrail's cultural picks
stories.summary: Piers McGrail is an IFTA-winning Irish cinematographer whose work spans film and television, with credits including Calm With Horses, Ordinary Love and It Is In Us All, for which he won the IFTA for Best Cinematography. Most recently, he served as director of photography on Everybody Digs Bill Evans, Grant Gee's jazz biopic written by Mark O'Halloran. The Irish-UK production premiered in Competition at this year's Berlin International Film Festival, where it won the Silver Bear for Best Director, one of the festival’s top prizes. I'll recommend a couple of great old films as I’m really slow to see the most recent ones. Sorcerer (by William Freidkin) encompasses so much that I enjoy in film - it’s a gritty and extremely tense thriller/adventure but it’s also weird and offbeat and fully of gritty atmosphere. And I’m a big Hitchcock fan so I’ll also recommend Foreign Correspondent, which is an early and lesser seen one (and clearly wartime propaganda) but very pacey and entertaining. Also, there's a re-release of Ken Russell’s The Devils coming up at the end of October, not to be missed. It features a manic Oliver Reed swinging around a taxidermied crocodile and an incredible performance from Vanessa Redgrave. And it’s visually stunning, with incredible production design at a scale that you rarely see in arthouse cinema. I hadn’t listened to Bill Evans much before working on the film but I emerged a convert and I’ve bought a bunch of his records since then. I’ve particularly enjoyed the 1970 album Alone.

stories.title: Sabrina Carpenter plays Jonathan Anderson in A24 x Dior project
stories.summary: Dior's Creative Director Jonathan Anderson shared an exciting message on Instagram yesterday afternoon, announcing a new creative collaboration between the French fashion house and indie film studio A24. The two-year partnership will take place through the A24-backed Cherry Lane Theatre in New York, kicking off with a one-night-only performance of "Both Ends", a stage production costumed by Anderson. Speaking on the collaboration, the designer said: "This is the start of an exciting partnership built around artists and storytelling. Putting two creatively driven worlds side by side - you start to see what they pull out of each other that neither could've found alone. That's where the interesting stuff happens." Teased by the Derry designer on Instagram, the 'A24 meets Dior' collab was announced through a celebrity-laden video featuring Sabrina Carpenter, Camille Cottin, Josh O'Connor, Drew Starkey, Sophie Wilde and, of course, Anderson himself. Directed by Aidan Zamiri, the short film saw the celebs audition to play Anderson, each giving their best impression of the Magherafelt native. Even Carpenter ditched her trademark heels and mini dresses for Anderson's signature look - a pair of jeans, a plaid shirt over a white T-shirt, and a comfortable pair of Salomon runners.

stories.title: Harris signals cut on heating oil tax, threshold rise
stories.summary: The Tánaiste has strongly suggested that the Government will cut tax on home heating oil in the Budget. The Government has two options when it comes to reducing the cost of home heating oil. It can lower the carbon tax on kerosene, something Sinn Féin is expected to introduce legislation on in the Dáil next week. Alternatively, it could equalise the VAT rate charged on home heating oil, which is currently 13.5%, with the 9% levied on gas. The latter approach has been proposed by the industry group, Fuels for Ireland. Mr Harris is also expected to commit today to increasing the threshold at which workers pay the higher rate of income tax in each of the next four budgets.

stories.title: 44% rise in heating oil price pushes up inflation up 3.7%
stories.summary: The rate of inflation in Ireland reached 3.7% in the 12 months to August, up from 3.4% in the year to July, new figures from the Central Statistics Office show today. The figures show the impact of higher oil prices with home heating oil up 44% over the past 12 months, while petrol prices rose by 9% and diesel jumped by 15%. The figures are based on the Consumer Price Index published by the Central Statistics Office. The CSO figures also show that clothing and footwear costs rose 3.6%. Education services rose by almost 9% because of a increase in costs associated with third-level education which came into effect from October 2025, the CSO said. However, food prices rose modestly by 0.1% overall. Meat rose by 2.2% while fish was up 3.3%, but milk and diary produce fell by 1.7%.

stories.title: Fines for social media firms counterproductive - minister
stories.summary: Minister for Communications Patrick O'Donovan has said that fines imposed on social media firms are "free advertising" for platforms and have become counterproductive. He was speaking at the opening of an EU Presidency conference in Dublin Castle on online safety which is hearing from policymakers, industry figures, representative organisations, regulators and children. Mr O'Donovan said Europe is moving towards stricter controls on social media and moving away from just imposing fines. "Fines are really important; the money goes back into the Exchequer," Mr O'Donovan said. "But these companies are gleaning enormous amounts of free advertising out of these fines, and it is actually, in many ways, becoming counterproductive," he added. The Communications Minister said that if the media regulator Coimisiún na Meán requests additional powers to ban platforms that are harmful to children, he would be open to considering it.

stories.title: Why are employers making you do so many rounds of job interviews?
stories.summary: Analysis: The move to get applicants to complete multiple interviews for jobs is another form of the conservative bias around hiring in many firms This article is now available as a Brainstorm podcast and can be heard above. You can also subscribe to the Brainstorm podcast through Apple Podcasts, Stitcher, Spotify or wherever you get your podcasts. The process of applying for jobs, especially jobs that involve any level of responsibility or reasonable pay, has become increasingly rigorous. It is not uncommon for applicants for managerial or technical jobs to go through many rounds of tests, assessments and interviews. Some of these are to assess qualifications and job-related skills and others to assess attitudes and cultural fit before a job offer is made. You might excel in test after test and in interview after interview, only to find that the organisation decides to go in a different direction at some point. It often looks like businesses are having a hard time making up their minds about applicants, and the trend to use multiple rounds of assessment appears to be growing. One of the reasons employers are taking so long in hiring is that they are increasingly likely to view full-time employees as liabilities rather than assets and new hires as a proposition that involves known costs but uncertain benefits. If you hire a new employee, you are liable for pay, benefits and the like, but you cannot be certain that the new employee will contribute to the organisation or fit the company culture. As a result, many large employers are reluctant to hire new employees or even to replace employees who depart. Organisational mission statements often include phrases like "employees are our most valuable asset" or "we treat employees as family", but the cold, hard truth is that many managers and executives wish they could get along without employees.

stories.title: Canada agrees significant air defence package for Ukraine
stories.summary: Canada has agreed a C$350 million (€218m) aid package for Kyiv to acquire air defence interceptors, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced, after meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Kyiv is running critically low on US-made Patriot interceptors capable of stopping Russia's ballistic missiles at a time when Moscow is stepping up its attacks. "As Russia escalates its barbaric aerial warfare indiscriminately targeting civilian populations, Ukraine's air defences are critical," Mr Carney told reporters in the Canadian city of Calgary. "Earlier today Canada and Ukraine finalised an agreement to deliver critical air defence interceptors ... this C$350 million equipment package will help protect Ukraine's people, infrastructure, and skies." He did not give details of which interceptors would be delivered or when the aid would start flowing. The weapons will be provided through a US programme that allows third party nations to quickly buy and supply weapons such as Patriot missiles to Ukraine.

Coincidentally, the top two and the bottom two are playing against one another, while the battle for fourth place is hotting up. Intriguingly, despite an inconsistent season, St Patrick's Athletic could be top of the table by 10pm on Monday evening. To do so, they need to pick up back-to-back wins, starting with current leaders, and defending champions, Shamrock Rovers later on. Pat's come into this latest Dublin derby off the back of their cup exit against Bohemians on Saturday. It seemed to have been written in the stars in a game in which Saints created numerous big chances, only for them to gift Bohs an own goal, before going out on penalties. They have seven league games left, and that's their lot for 2026. Could they pull off the most unlikely of league titles by the end of October?

stories.title: Minister for Sport wants 'realistic' integration deadline
stories.summary: Minister for Sport Patrick O'Donovan said he wants to see "realistic" and "achievable" deadlines in place for the amalgamation of the GAA, LGFA and Camogie Association. Earlier today, GAA president Jarlath Burns admitted that the stalling of integration is due to financial concerns at the top level of Gaelic games in equally funding male and female teams. Dr Mary McAleese, the former President of Ireland, yesterday stood down as chairperson of the Integration Committee overseeing the amalgamation of the GAA, LGFA and Camogie Association. McAleese cited changes to agreed timelines, a GAA management committee that she described as "less than impressive", and her feeling that there were "people who are not entirely happy about the idea of including women in decision-making at the top level of Gaelic sports" who were holding the process back. "It is far better to get this right than to rush it," he said. Ryan has written to GAA clubs across the country to reaffirm the organisation's "commitment to deliver integration for the wider Gaelic games family".

stories.title: Liverpool come from behind to see off Atletico
stories.summary: A day after pledging his full commitment to Liverpool despite his sadness at their failure to offer him a new contract Mac Allister duly delivered with a brilliant winning goal against Atletico Madrid. The Argentina international stressed he would give 100% to the cause despite the perceived slight and was true to his word with a sweetly-struck left-footed effort from 20 yards. That came after Dominik Szoboszlai's equaliser had cancelled out Liverpool nemesis Marcos Llorente’s fifth goal in three Anfield visits as head coach Andoni Iraola celebrated his managerial Champions League debut with a 2-1 win. Mac Allister’s all-round performance was one of many positives, as was the full debut of £106million signing Bradley Barcola who, with better finishing would have had a hat-trick before he was forced off with an apparent calf injury. Florian Wirtz, one of the great hopes of last summer’s window, continued his improvement and seemed to find the France international’s wavelength pretty quickly. Barcola, back-to-back Champions League winner with Paris St Germain, started on the right rather than his preferred left with Cody Gakpo left out as a precaution and twice shot at goalkeeper Jan Oblak from promising positions in the first half.

stories.title: True Dub Flood excited for rugby's Tallaght debut
stories.summary: Having togged out in green at the Aviva Stadium, Ringsend native Stacey Flood has said she cannot wait for Ireland's Tallaght debut on Sunday, 20 September. By her own admission, Flood is a true Dub, steeped in a Dublin sporting family. Her sister Kim also represented Leinster and Ireland in rugby as well as the Dublin ladies Gaelic footballers. That passion is present in the stands, meaning the Ireland full-back is expecting the full clan to turn out when Ireland play host to the USA. Speaking at the launch of the IRFU's new men's and women's jerseys last week, the 30-year-old could not withhold her excitement for the latest road trip of this team's tour around the country. "It feels like I'm playing at home every time I play in Dublin and throughout my career, I didn't get to do that often, playing sevens; so, every time we play in Dublin, I know half the Flood family is going to be there, even when we play everywhere else actually, they're always there. "I feel like everyone has their communities, like Béibhinn (Parsons) and Aoibheann (Reilly) being from Galway, they get so (much) support there and I feel like I'm not a country girl, I'm like everyone in Dublin supports me. "They might not know me but that's how I make it in my head, I'm like everyone's there to support me because I'm a Dub. I feel like it's different in the country, but I just try to replicate that for Dublin for myself."

stories.title: Marvel's Wolverine reviewed – a superhero game with claws
stories.summary: Marvel's Wolverine is a single-player action game that catapults one of the most iconic X-Men into a long-overdue gaming spotlight. Offering astonishingly brutal combat, an abundance of heavyweight cameos, and an emotionally charged storyline that will claw at your heartstrings, this game has everything you need from a superhero experience. Make no mistake, bub. This is Wolverine at his bloodiest, most brutal, and best. And the potential this game brings to realising a wider X-Men universe in video games is something I think fans should be very excited about. Marvel's Wolverine introduces a brand-new story that balances familiarity with ambition. You may know and love the characters featured, but the game is unafraid to take them in new directions you can’t help but be engrossed by. Wolverine is a character I’ve always felt was uncomfortable with the moniker of 'superhero'. This is understandable, given the unchecked violence we know he is capable of committing. But I will be honest when I say I was taken aback by just how well the game delves between mindless combat and the deeper tragedy of the character's background.

stories.title: Christian Siriano's NYFW show was a twisted take on a fairy tale
stories.summary: Christian Siriano brought his twist on a French fairytale fantasy to New York Fashion Week with a theatrical collection featuring dramatic corsets, florals and clouds of tulle. The American designer, known for dressing stars including Zendaya, Celine Dion and Oprah Winfrey, unveiled his spring/summer 2027 collection at Gotham Hall in Manhattan on Thursday. Siriano drew inspiration from the 18th-century French fairytale The Story Of The Queen Of The Flowery Isles, using its darker themes before transforming the runway into a colourful floral fantasy. The show began on a decidedly darker note, with models showcasing black lace, feathers and faux leather, while a male model walking the runway in a fitted, sheer top paired with loose silk trousers. The sombre palette reflected the darker side of the fairytale, which deals with themes including vanity, rivalry and revenge, before the collection gradually gave way to a softer and more romantic world. "I think fashion needs that," Siriano told the Associated Press of creating fantasy through clothes. "I think people need a little bit of escape."

stories.title: Senior officer to lead probe into fatal three-car crash
stories.summary: A senior investigating officer has been appointed to lead an investigation into the death of a man following a three-car crash in Co Meath last month. A man, aged in his 50s, sustained critical injuries following the collision on the R132 at Smithstown in Julianstown in the early hours of Saturday 15 August. He later died from his injuries in Our Lady of Lourdes Hospital Drogheda on Friday 4 September. Gardaí last month said the man had been injured while standing at the rear of his vehicle, after being pulled in to the side of the road following a collision with another vehicle 10 minutes earlier. A third vehicle then collided with the rear of his vehicle and he was seriously injured. In a statement this morning, gardaí said a family liaison officer has been appointed to support the family of the deceased, and a senior investigating officer will lead the investigation.

stories.title: Keys to World Trade Centre to go on display in Cavan
stories.summary: Keys to the World Trade Centre are among artefacts belonging to 9/11 survivor and Cavan man Hugh Smith that will go on display in the county this weekend. Hugh Smith, who is originally from Termon in Cavan, survived the collapse of the Twin Towers but became a prominent figure in the rescue and clean-up effort. He had made Warwick, New York, his home and as a carpenter, worked on the construction of the World Trade Centre and continued to work there in maintenance for 27 years until the 2001 terrorist attack. He helped other survivors to escape and then dedicated the following weeks and months to the recovery operation. Hugh Smith died in April 2025, but before his death, he bequeathed some of his most cherished mementos of the World Trade Centre to the Cavan County Museum, which is hosting an exhibition to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the September 11th attacks. The items on display include a cross fashioned from the building's steel girders, keys to the World Trade Centre itself and his hard hat, which he wore through the recovery effort.

stories.title: PBP propose data centre levy to fund €500 energy credit
stories.summary: People Before Profit-Solidarity has proposed that data centres should be forced to pay the same percentage of tax on their electricity as ordinary households. Outlining the proposal at the party's think-in in Dublin this afternoon, it said the €1.5 billion raised from the move would be used to fund a €500 energy credit for homes and additional funding for disability services. Under the plans, which will be tabled in a private members motion in the Dáil next week, the party wants to double the amount of tax data centres pay on their electricity to be doubled from 20c per KWh to 40c per KWh - the same amount as an ordinary household. Outlining the proposal to reporters, PBP-Solidarity TD Paul Murphy said the move would raise €1.5bn extra for the exchequer every year, and would be used to fund a €500 energy credit and for homes as well as extra funding and supports for children with disabilities. "Data centres pay half the price for the electricity they use. We would use that money [the €1.5bn fund] to shield people from the cost-of-living crisis." Party members also said they want to see a wealth tax introduced in the upcoming budget which would target individuals with a net worth of €5m or more, which the party said would raise €9bn for the exchequer which could be re-routed to fund other areas.

stories.title: 1.2 billion payments worth €50bn made on Irish cards
stories.summary: More than 1.2 billion domestic payments were made on Irish cards, valued at almost €50 billion, in the first half of 2026, new figures from Banking & Payments Federation Ireland show today. The latest Payments Monitor from BPFI reveals that 75.3% of these payments were made at the point of sale (POS) in shops, restaurants and other retail outlets, increasing by 5.4% in volume year on year to 930 million transactions. BPFI noted that 89.9% of POS payments were contactless, with mobile wallets accounting for almost two thirds of contactless payments. A total of 153 contactless payments per person were conduced in Ireland on Irish cards in the first half of 2026, up from 143 the same time last year. Dublin recorded the highest number of contactless payments per capita in Ireland, at 419 in the 12 months to June, including 279 made through mobile wallets. Carlow had the second highest number of contactless and mobile wallet payments per capita, at 355 and 208 respectively, followed by Limerick, with 324 contactless and 203 mobile wallet payments per capita.

stories.title: Houthis take Yemeni port city, threaten Saudi oil exports
stories.summary: Iran-aligned Houthis have seized control of Yemen's port city of Mocha and advanced down the Red Sea coast to strategic islands, military sources said, hours after President Donald Trump said he expected the Iran war to end after midterm elections. Yemeni government military sources said the Houthis had gained further leverage over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the southern outlet of the Red Sea and one of the world's most important shipping routes, and had reached the islands of Hanish. Red Sea navigation is safe for all shipping companies except for Saudi vessels, Yemen's Houthi-run humanitarian operations coordination centre said in a statement. Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil exporter, has relied on the Red Sea shipping route since the Iran conflict effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil used to flow. Houthi spokesperson Mohammed Abdulsalam said, without elaborating, that operations were defensive and would stop once attacks on Yemen stopped. If the Houthis were to impose a stranglehold over the waterway, on the opposite side of the Arabian peninsula from the Strait of Hormuz, it could give their sponsor Iran a critical advantage in the war with the US, reducing supplies through a second major transit corridor and sending oil prices surging.

stories.title: 49ers demolish rival Rams in NFL's Australian debut
stories.summary: The San Francisco 49ers dominated the Los Angeles Rams 27-7 in front of more than 100,000 fans at the Melbourne Cricket Ground on Friday morning. Both sides took vastly different travel strategies ahead of the first-ever regular season NFL game in Australia. The 49ers arrived in Melbourne a week before the game, while the Rams spent just over 24 hours Down Under before the 10.30am kick-off. San Francisco were able to get on the scoreboard first with a field goal in the opening quarter, but it was not until the second quarter that the game began to open up. A rushing touchdown to Kyren Williams gave the Rams a four-point advantage, before an interception by the Rams a few minutes later threatened to sink San Francisco. However, the 49ers defence was able to hold out until Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford threw a pick of his own. San Francisco were finally able to find the end zone four minutes from half-time on a perfectly weighted deep ball from Brock Purdy to Demarcus Robinson.
